title: Scientists Test a Nuclear Plan to Stop a Giant Asteroid
summary: Imagine a space rock too big for a gentle push to move in time. Scientists are testing what to do about that kind of rock with computer models, not real explosions. About 66 million years ago, the asteroid Chicxulub, about 6 to 9 miles wide, hit Earth and wiped out about 75 percent of life, including all non-avian dinosaurs. Nothing that big has hit since, but scientists say another big hit is not impossible. In 2022, NASA's DART mission hit Dimorphos, the small moon of the asteroid Didymos, and changed its orbit. But Didymos was small and was never a threat. For a much bigger rock with very little warning time, many impactors would be impractical. So a team at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, led by physicist Isaiah Santisevan, simulated a nuclear device exploding above the asteroid. Its X-rays would heat the surface until it vaporizes, pushing the rock the other way. In the longest simulation, the asteroid broke apart, and most of its pieces moved faster than its escape velocity. Scientists need to track where those pieces would go.
why_it_matters: Learning how scientists protect Earth from space rocks shows how math and computers can solve huge problems before they happen.

background_read: An asteroid is a space rock that orbits the Sun.
About 66 million years ago, a very large one hit Earth and wiped out about 75 percent of life.
Scientists test plans with computer models instead of real explosions, including using X-rays to heat a rock's surface until it vaporizes and pushes the rock away.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists, a team at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory led by physicist Isaiah Santisevan, and NASA.
WHAT: Testing a nuclear plan to stop a giant asteroid using computer models, not real explosions.
WHERE: In computer models on Earth, for asteroids in space.
WHY: A gentle push may not move a very big rock in time, so scientists test stronger options.
